title: Problem Statement and Survey of Known Results
content: Header documentation establishing Erdős Problem #1142: are there infinitely many n such that n − 2^k is prime for all 1 < 2^k < n? The known values are n ∈ {4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105} (OEIS A039669). Mientka & Weitzenkamp (1969) verified no other n ≤ 2^{44} satisfy this. Vaughan (1973) showed the count of such n up to N is extremely sparse. Erdős conjectured the number of primes of the form n − 2^k is o(log n), which would imply only finitely many n satisfy the full property.
mathContext: The problem asks: is $\{n \in \mathbb{N} : n - 2^k \text{ prime for all } 1 < 2^k < n\}$ infinite? Known elements: $\{4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105\}$. Computational search to $2^{44}$ found no others.

title: Core Definitions: powersOfTwoBetween and SatisfiesErdos1142
content: `powersOfTwoBetween n` computes the finite set {2^k : k ≥ 1, 2^k < n} by filtering exponents in Finset.range n and mapping through 2^(·). `SatisfiesErdos1142 n` requires (1) this set is nonempty (n ≥ 4, since 2^1 = 2 < 4) and (2) n − m is prime for every m in the set. The `Decidable` instance enables computational verification via `native_decide`. The definition uses universal quantification over a finite set, making it both mathematically precise and computationally tractable.
mathContext: $\text{SatisfiesErdos1142}(n) \iff \{2^k : 1 \leq k,\, 2^k < n\} \neq \emptyset \land \forall m \in \{2^k : 2^k < n\},\, (n-m) \text{ is prime}$

title: Computational Verification of OEIS A039669
content: Seven theorems verify each element of OEIS A039669 satisfies the property, all proved by `native_decide`. For n = 105 (the largest known), the powers of 2 in (1, 105) are {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}, and 105 minus each gives {103, 101, 97, 89, 73, 41} — all prime. The increasing number of primality conditions (from 1 for n=4 to 6 for n=105) illustrates why larger solutions become exponentially harder to find: n must simultaneously satisfy ⌋log₂ n⌋ primality tests.

title: Structural Properties: n ≥ 4, Parity, and n − 2 Prime
content: `erdos1142_ge_4` proves n ≥ 4 by extracting an element from powersOfTwoBetween (existence gives n ≥ 3, then primality of n−2 gives n−2 ≥ 2, so n ≥ 4). `erdos1142_n_minus_2_prime` shows n−2 is always prime (since 2 ∈ powersOfTwoBetween n for n ≥ 3). `erdos1142_odd_or_4` proves parity: if n > 4 is even, then n−2 is even and ≥ 4, contradicting primality. The proof uses `Prime.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd` to show that 2 | (n−2) with n−2 prime forces n−2 = 2, hence n = 4. `erdos1142_mod2` packages this as n % 2 = 1 for n > 4.
mathContext: Structural constraints: (1) $n \geq 4$ (need $2 < n$). (2) $n - 2$ is prime. (3) For $n > 4$: $n$ is odd (if even, $n-2$ even and $\geq 4$, not prime). These reduce the search space to odd $n \geq 7$.

title: The Open Conjecture and Stronger Quantitative Version
content: `erdos_1142_conjecture` states the main open problem as `Set.Infinite {n : ℕ | SatisfiesErdos1142 n}`. `erdos_1142_stronger_conjecture` formalizes Erdős's quantitative conjecture: for every ε > 0, for sufficiently large n, the count of k with n − 2^k prime is at most ε · log₂(n). This o(log n) bound on the prime count would imply that eventually no n can satisfy ALL ⌋log₂ n⌋ conditions simultaneously, suggesting the set {4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105} is complete. The formal statement uses Finset.filter.card cast to ℝ and compared with ε · Nat.log 2 n.
mathContext: **Main conjecture**: $|\{n : \text{SatisfiesErdos1142}(n)\}| = \infty$? **Stronger conjecture**: $|\{k : 1 \leq k,\, 2^k < n,\, n-2^k \text{ prime}\}| = o(\log_2 n)$. If the stronger conjecture holds with $\varepsilon = 1/2$, then for large $n$, prime count $\leq \frac{1}{2}\log_2 n < \lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, so not ALL differences can be prime.

title: Completeness Verification and Relationship to Problem #236
content: `erdos1142_complete_le_105` proves computationally (via `native_decide`) that the set of n ≤ 105 satisfying the property is exactly {4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105}. This verifies the OEIS data by exhaustive search over Finset.range 106. The file documents the logical implication from the stronger conjecture to finiteness: taking ε = 1/2, for large n the prime count ≤ (1/2)·log₂(n) < ⌋log₂(n−1)⌋ = |powersOfTwoBetween n|, so not all differences can be prime. This proof sketch is blocked by the Nat.log/Finset.card/ℝ arithmetic bridge.
mathContext: $\{n \leq 105 : \text{SatisfiesErdos1142}(n)\} = \{4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105\}$ (exhaustive search). The TODO connects to Problem #236 via: $\varepsilon = 1/2 \Rightarrow$ prime count $< \lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ for large $n$, contradicting the full property.
